newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels challenge Zaire plan to retake seized land.
newsitem.headline: Rebels challenge Zaire plan to retake seized land.

text.p: Zaire's badly paid, indisciplined army looks unlikely to soon be able to retake eastern borderlands seized by rebels, aid workers and analysts said on Tuesday.
Facing both lack of discipline from within its own ranks and a widening rebel front, the Zaire army's much touted counter-offensive looks unrealistic in the short term.
"After two months of defeats, morale amongst the soldiers is very low," said a Western analyst in the capital Kinshasa.

"Unless President Mobutu returns from France, places a real military man at the top, and hires outside help to train and fight alongside the regular army, the rebel offensive may continue to spread," added the analyst, who has spent years in Zaire.
President Mobutu Sese Seko has been away since August for cancer treatment in Europe and his expected return last week failed to materialise. There is now no word on his homecoming.

In reports on the fighting, local authorities said the crumbling jungle city of Kisangani remained under Zaire army control despite rebel claims of entering it. Aid workers also doubted the rebel claims.
Commander Jean Kabongo, special security adviser to rebel leader Laurent Kabila, told Reuters in the town of Goma that both Bunia and Walikale had fallen to rebel forces.
Kabongo said on Monday that the rebels, known as the Alliance of Democratic Forces, had captured parts of Kisangani, but aid agencies said on Tuesday the city remained in government hands.
The commander repeated his claim on Tuesday. "We are in and around Kisangani... There will be a big combat for Kisangani but our forces have been there, around it, for a month," he said.

There is only one passable road to Kisangani from the east. The road crossses the town of Lubutu which, according to aid workers who were there at the weekend, is in the hands of Zaire's best trained troops, the Presidential Guard.
However, the rebel claim, may at least raise tension in advance of an attack on Kisangani.

Before the eastern towns of Goma and Bukavu were captured in early November, Rwandan-backed rebels announced their arrival in advance, spreading panic amongst both the population and the ill-equipped Zairean troops stationed there.
Already Kisangani has suffered from three weeks of sporadic looting by army deserters who arrived in the city having fled fighting in the east.
"The local population is now organising itself to disarm uncontrolled soldiers," said Alphonse Toko of the U.N. children's agencey UNICEF.
"Last Saturday there was also a military operation to disarm them and bring them under control," added Toko, who returned from Kisangani on Monday.

The Zaire government itself is under pressure from opponents in Kinshasa, including senior ranking military officers who have organised numerous well-attended street demonstrations in an attempt to topple Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.
The government at the weekend accused Uganda of using tanks and other armoured vehicles to capture the towns of Beni and Kasindi, just over 200 km (120 miles) from Goma city.
A Zairean military source said on Monday authorities were weighing how best to respond to the attacks by Ugandan troops.
But missionary sources said on Monday Beni had been captured by Zairean rebels.
